capstone: Run a full analyst engagement against your home lab: (1) scope and scan it with a vulnerability scanner, (2) monitor it for one week with your SIEM and triage every alert, (3) simulate an intrusion, execute the IR lifecycle, and preserve evidence properly, (4) deliver two polished documents — a vulnerability assessment report and an incident report with remediation plan — written for a non-technical stakeholder. Present both reports as if to a hiring manager; the capstone is complete when a peer can follow your methodology from scope to recommendation without asking clarifying questions.

checkpoints: Explain, in your own words, the difference between a worm and a trojan, and give one realistic containment step for each.
Given an nmap result showing SMBv1 open on a workstation, name the risk and the two fastest mitigations.
Draft three bullet-point social-engineering red flags you would teach a non-technical employee.
keyConcepts: Threat actor types: nation-state, hacktivist, organized crime, insider
Social engineering: phishing, vishing, smishing, pretexting, watering-hole
Malware classes: ransomware, trojan, worm, rootkit, keylogger, logic bomb
Application attacks: injection, XSS, directory traversal, replay
Network attacks: MITM, DoS/DDoS, DNS poisoning, rogue APs
Vulnerability feeds and advisories (CVE, vendor bulletins)
Attack surface and the kill-chain concept
labs: Recon lab: from a Kali VM, run nmap -sV -O against a lab target (your own router's LAN side or a Metasploitable/VM target you own) and document every open service with a one-line risk note.
Phishing triage drill: collect five real phishing samples from a public phishing corpus, then build a checklist of header/body indicators and score each sample.
Malware taxonomy table: build a comparison table of eight malware classes with infection vector, persistence mechanism, and detection hint for each.
Home attack-surface audit: enumerate every device on your home LAN, list open ports, and write a two-paragraph prioritized hardening list.
objectives: Classify threat actors by motivation, capability, and resources and explain how each shapes an organization's risk picture.
Describe common attack families — social engineering, malware types, application attacks, network attacks — and how they achieve initial access.
Explain vulnerability research sources and why patching, hardening, and configuration management matter.
Run a safe reconnaissance lab against your own home network and identify exposed services.

checkpoints: Draw the shared-responsibility split for a database running on a cloud VM vs. a managed database service.

Apply defense-in-depth: segmentation, zoning, DMZ, and firewall placement in a small-network diagram.

checkpoints: Explain why passwords are hashed and salted rather than encrypted, and what goes wrong without a salt.
Describe what a certificate chain proves and what OCSP is for.
List the legacy wireless protocols you would never deploy today and why.

labs: OpenSSL PKI lab: create your own root CA with OpenSSL, issue a server certificate, then revoke it and verify the revocation status.
Hashing lab: hash the same file with two algorithms, change one byte, and document how the digest changes; then salt and hash a test password.
Wireshark crypto lab: capture an HTTPS session and an SSH session; identify the handshake phases and the cipher suite negotiated.
Router hardening: audit your own Wi-Fi configuration (encryption standard, WPS, guest network, admin password) and apply fixes.

checkpoints: Name the six phases of the incident response lifecycle and one deliverable each phase produces.

checkpoints: Explain why a credentialed scan finds more than a non-credentialed one, and one risk of credentialed scanning.
Given a critical finding on an internet-facing host and a high finding on an isolated test VM, justify your fix order.
Describe what must be in a penetration test's rules of engagement before testing begins.

checkpoints: Walk an alert from initial detection to escalation decision, naming what a tier-1 analyst documents at each step.
Explain the difference between a false positive and a benign positive with an example.
Describe how you would tune a rule that fires 500 times a day on legitimate admin activity.

checkpoints: Your monitoring shows active data exfiltration: argue for immediate isolation vs. continued observation, then state which you choose and why.
